name: Live blood analysis

lead: Live blood analysis (LBA) examines an unstained drop of finger-prick blood under a dark-field microscope, often shown on a screen to the client. Practitioners say it reveals nutritional status, toxicity, immune function, acidity and yeast, and they recommend diets and supplements in response, framed as steps toward better energy, clearer skin and a healthier look.

The practice rests on pleomorphism theory from Günther Enderlein in the 1920s. Studies have found it unreliable for diagnosis, and a 2017 study reported that the bacteria-like structures seen are non-living vesicles and protein particles.

paras: A sample is taken, viewed live, and findings such as clumped cells or particles are explained to the client with a supplement or dietary plan, sometimes with a follow-up sample to show change.

Reviews and regulators report that findings are not reliable for diagnosis, and a UK Committee of Advertising Practice statement restricted advertising of it.[1] Cases include a 2002 Australian naturopath fined after a patient's death and 2014 UK Cancer Act convictions.[1]

angle.text: People undergo the test hoping to learn what is limiting their health and appearance and to receive a supplement plan. Practitioners say the images motivate and guide dietary changes.

lead: Live blood analysis, also called live cell analysis, uses high-resolution dark-field microscopy on a living blood sample. Practitioners such as nutritionists, naturopaths and chiropractors say it shows immune status, vitamin deficiencies, toxicity, pH and mineral imbalances, and fungus or yeast.[1]

The method traces to Günther Enderlein's pleomorphism theories of around 1925; Robert O. Young later promoted it.[1][2] Its link to looks is through the supplement and diet programmes sold after a session, which are presented as improving health, energy and skin.

Studies in 2005 and 2006 found dark-field microscopy could not detect cancer and that LBA lacked reliability.[1] A 2017 Scientific Reports paper showed that bacteria-like structures in healthy blood under dark-field are non-living vesicles and protein particles.[3]

paras: Enderlein's 1925 book Bakterien-Cyklogenie proposed that microbes pass through forms within the blood, in opposition to the monomorphic germ theory; the pleomorphic idea drew on earlier work by Antoine Béchamp.[2]
The finger-prick sample is viewed unstained. Interpreters read stacked red cells (rouleaux), particles and crystals as indicators of acidity, toxins or parasites, and recommend supplements.[1]

Researchers report that rouleaux arise from drying or clotting, and that glass shards and debris have been read as crystals or parasites; Edzard Ernst and Andrew Weil have criticised the method.[1] A 2007 Dutch commentary placed LBA among alternative diagnostic methods that can yield incorrect diagnoses.[4]
Regulatory actions include Pennsylvania in 1996, Rhode Island in 2005 and the UK CAP in 2013; Robert O. Young was charged in 2014 and Errol Denton was convicted in the UK in 2014 and 2018.[1]

Studies in 2005 (El-Safadi) and 2006 (Teut) tested dark-field microscopy and found it could not detect cancer and lacked reproducibility and sensitivity.[1] The 2017 study identified the bacteria-like forms as vesicles and protein particles that increase with incubation.[3]

lore.intro: LBA is discussed in alternative-health communities as a window into hidden health problems.
